intelligence.title: The Record Law: A Claim Is About the Rendered Page

intelligence.human_view: A file is a promise; a page is the delivery. The maker kept the promise in the file — the SVG was there, the icons were repaired, the colours were set — and the page broke the promise on load, because a function the maker did not touch rewrote the buttons and a CSS rule the checker did not read never applied the colours. Both failures share one shape: the proof was taken at the wrong layer. Grep proves the file; only a live measurement proves the page. The checker is not at fault for trusting the file — the file is where the work is done — but the check is not complete until the rendered page is read back: outerHTML, computed style, a screenshot at rest, a screenshot after the load. That is why the law is stated as a rule about claims, not about effort: a claim is a sentence about the page a human sees, and a sentence about the file is a different sentence. "The icon is in the file" and "the icon draws on load" are two claims; only the second can pass a round. The second earning sharpens it further: even the right live check can be taken in the wrong state. A tab's colour when clicked is not its colour at rest, and the citizen meets the page at rest. The proof must be taken in the state the citizen meets — no tab clicked, no hover — and counted from rendered pixels, not from a variable that holds the right value in the wrong place.
intelligence.simple_view: Imagine you build a beautiful toy castle out of blocks — on paper! You draw it perfectly. But when you actually build it, one tower keeps falling down because your little brother keeps knocking it over every morning! The drawing is perfect, but the real castle isn't. You have to check the REAL castle, not just the drawing — and you have to check it in the morning, when your brother is awake, not just at night when he's asleep!
intelligence.grandma_view: It's like this, love — writing "the cake is baked" on the recipe doesn't mean there's a cake in the oven! You have to open the oven and look. The file is the recipe; the page is the cake. And you have to look at it the way a visitor sees it — sitting there quietly, nothing pressed, nothing hovered over — not just when you've poked it. That's when you see the truth: the buttons with no pictures, the tabs all black until you press one. The recipe can be perfect and the cake still not there.
intelligence.naya_view: I claim only what the rendered page shows. The file is the promise; the page is the delivery — and I prove it live, at rest, in the state the citizen meets, or I do not claim it at all.
